title: Trader, researcher, developer
objectives: Tell the three quant roles apart by their daily work and by what their interviews test.

screens.prose: As of 2 November 2026, summer 2027 offers are landing and some first-year deadlines are 6 days away. First you need to know which job you are applying for.

state.caption: Drag each task to the person who does it most days.

screens.question: Sort the nine tasks into the three jobs.

hints.text: Who is on the phone to the market, who is in the data, and who is in the code?
These three happen while the market is open and money is at risk.
Trader: quote, size, hedge. Researcher: fit, test, clean. Developer: latency, pricer, crash.

feedback.correct: Three people, three kinds of day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask who works with money at risk, who works with data, and who writes code.

byKey.pricer: You put the pricer with the researcher. The researcher designs the maths; the developer builds the code that runs it every day.
byKey.clean: Cleaning a dataset is the start of research. A model is only as good as the data under it.
byKey.size: Sizing a bet is a trader's call: how much to risk on a price they believe in.
byKey.signal: Testing a signal is research: does this pattern predict returns on data it has not seen?
byKey.latency: Cutting latency is engineering: making the system answer in fewer microseconds.
byKey.quote: Quoting a price is the trader's core task, many times a minute.
byKey.hedge: Hedging removes risk the trader does not want to hold. That is a trading decision.
byKey.fit: Fitting a model to data is research.
byKey.crash: Fixing a crash in a live system is a developer's job.

explain.text: The trader acts on prices with money at risk. The researcher works in data to find what predicts prices. The developer builds the code both of them rely on.

screens.prose: You sorted by daily work. A **trader** prices and takes risk. A **researcher** finds and tests ideas in data. A **developer** builds the systems. Interviews test what the job needs.
screens.question: Which set of tests fits the trader's row?

options.text: Mental arithmetic, probability, expected value and market-making games
Accounting, company valuation and the news
options.why: You matched the job to finance knowledge. A trader is tested on fast, careful numbers and bets, not on accounts.

options.text: Coding at speed and data structures
options.why: You picked the developer's tests. A trader writes little code in the interview.

options.text: Regression and an open data case
options.why: You picked the researcher's tests. A trader decides in seconds, so the tests are fast.

hints.text: What does a trader do many times a minute?
A quote is a price you will buy and sell at.
Quoting needs quick arithmetic, probability and expected value. Interviews test exactly those.

feedback.correct: Quick numbers and good bets: the trader's day in an interview.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the tests to the trader's daily work.

explain.text: A trader's day is pricing and betting under time pressure. So interviews test mental arithmetic, probability, expected value and live market-making games.

screens.prose: Now the researcher's row. A researcher spends weeks on one question in data.
screens.question: Which set of tests fits the researcher's row?

options.text: Statistics, regression, machine learning, an open data case and coding
Mental arithmetic and market-making games only
options.why: You gave the researcher the trader's tests. Research is judged on careful work with data, not on speed alone.
You assumed a research interview is a finance exam. It tests statistics and data skills.

options.text: C++ memory management and operating systems
options.why: You picked the developer's systems tests. Researchers code, but in Python and on data.

hints.text: What tools does a researcher use to test a signal?
A dataset, a model and a test on unseen data.
Statistics, regression, machine learning, coding, and an open case built on data.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the tests to a day spent in data.

explain.text: A researcher's work is careful inference from data. Interviews test statistics, regression, machine learning and coding, often with an open case.

screens.prose: Last, the developer's row. A developer's code runs the firm's trading all day.
screens.question: Which set of tests fits the developer's row?

options.text: Coding at speed and data structures; at some firms C++ and systems
Market-making games and dice puzzles only
options.why: You gave the developer the trader's tests. A developer is hired to write correct, fast code.

options.text: An open data case on house prices
options.why: You gave the developer the researcher's case. Developer rounds are coding rounds.
Every role gets behavioural questions, but you skipped the technical core.

hints.text: What would go wrong if a developer were weak?
The code is the job.
Coding at speed, data structures and, at low-latency firms, C++ and systems.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the tests to a day spent building systems.

explain.text: A developer's work is code that must be right and fast. Interviews test coding at speed and data structures, with C++ and systems at some firms.

screens.prose: A posting from an invented London trading firm lists the intern's tasks. Read the tasks and decide which tests to expect.

columns: The posting says the intern will
rows: Quote prices on an exchange through the day
Manage the risk of the positions they build
Join a daily trading game with the other interns
Work beside researchers who improve the models

state.caption: An invented firm. The tasks are what matter.

screens.question: Select all that apply: which tests should this candidate expect?

options.why: You read "work beside researchers" as a coding job. The intern quotes and manages risk: a trader's tasks.
You chose a researcher's test. Working beside researchers does not make the intern one.

hints.text: Three of the four lines describe one role.
Quoting and managing risk.
These are trader tasks, so expect trader tests: arithmetic, probability and a market-making game.

feedback.correct: A trader's tasks, so a trader's tests.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each task to a role, then take that role's tests.

explain.text: Quoting, managing risk and a trading game are a trader's day. So the tests are arithmetic, probability, expected value and a market-making game.

screens.prose: Some banks call their desk quants **strats**: Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, as reported, October 2026 (sources in l4). A strat builds models and the code that runs them.
screens.question: Which mix is closest to a strats interview?

options.text: Researcher and developer: probability and maths with coding

options.why: You matched "desk" to trading. Strats build models and code for the desk; reports describe probability and coding rounds.
You read the bank title as client work. Strats are quants, tested on maths and code.

options.text: No technical questions at a bank
options.why: You assumed banks skip technical rounds. Reported strats processes include coding and maths tests.

hints.text: A strat builds models and the code that runs them.
Models are research; code is development.
A hybrid: probability and maths like a researcher, coding like a developer.

feedback.correct: A hybrid of researcher and developer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a strat builds.

explain.text: A strat builds models and the code that runs them, so the interviews mix probability and maths with coding. As reported, October 2026; l4 has the firm-by-firm detail and sources.

screens.prose: A friend has a trading interview next month. Her plan is to read up on derivatives and Black-Scholes first.

rows: Open to people without a finance background

state.caption: Check the firm's own page before acting.

screens.question: What should she prepare first?

options.text: Mental arithmetic, probability and expected value
Derivatives and Black-Scholes, then the rest
options.why: You prepared finance knowledge first. Trading firms state that no finance knowledge is needed; they test numbers and bets.
You prepared for a markets chat. The technical rounds are arithmetic, probability and games.
You prepared facts about the firm. That helps one fit question at most.

hints.text: Read what the firms themselves say.
Both lines say the same thing.
No finance knowledge is needed. Prepare what the job uses: arithmetic, probability, expected value.

feedback.correct: Firms train the finance. They test the thinking.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read what the firms state about finance knowledge.

byKey.deriv: You chose derivatives first. Trading firms state that no finance knowledge is needed, so that time is better spent on arithmetic and probability.

explain.text: IMC and SIG state that interns need no finance background (October 2026). Their rounds test arithmetic, probability and games. Sources: IMC Trader Intern posting, imc.com; SIG Quantitative Trading Internship listing, efinancialcareers.com.

screens.prose: Two invented firms post jobs with the same title, "Quantitative Trader". Read what each one does.

rows: Write and test systematic strategies in Python; watch them run live
Quote prices by hand on an exchange; manage risk through the day

screens.question: Which posting's interviews will lean on statistics and coding?

options.why: You chose the hand-quoting job. Its tasks are a trader's, so expect arithmetic and games.

options.text: Both, since the title is the same
options.why: You read the title, not the tasks. One title can hide two different jobs.

options.text: Neither; traders are never tested on coding
options.why: You trusted the word "trader". Firm X's tasks are research and code.

hints.text: Ignore the title for a moment.
Writing and testing strategies in Python.
Firm X does research and code under a trading title. Its interviews will look like a researcher's.

feedback.correct: Read the tasks, not the title.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the tasks, not the titles.

explain.text: Firm X's tasks are a researcher's and a developer's: strategies in Python, tested on data. Firm Y's are a trader's. The title is the same; the jobs and the interviews differ.

screens.prose: Turn what you did into a routine for any posting.
screens.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Read the tasks in the posting
Match each task to trader, researcher or developer
List what that role's interviews test
Plan your preparation from that list
Choose by the title that sounds best
lines.why: You chose by title. One title can mean two jobs, as Firm X and Firm Y showed.

hints.text: What did you look at for Firm X and Firm Y?
The tasks come first; the tests follow from the role.
Read the tasks, match them to a role, list its tests, then plan. The title line does not belong.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step uses the one before it.

byKey.title: You kept the title step. The title can mislead; the tasks decide the role.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step that belongs. Only the title line goes.

explain.text: The tasks tell you the role, and the role tells you the tests. That list is your preparation plan. A title alone can point the wrong way.

screens.prose: A maths student enjoys fast mental games and plays poker with friends. She likes quick decisions with an answer the same day. The course leads with trader and researcher examples. Developer depth comes in Coding Interviews and Systems for Developer Interviews (later in the course list).
screens.question: Which role's interviews suit her best?

options.why: You picked the role of long questions and data. She enjoys quick decisions with fast feedback, which is a trader's day.
Nothing she enjoys is about building code. A developer's interviews are coding rounds.
Not sure is a fair answer for you, but her description points clearly to one role.

hints.text: Which interviews feature mental games and bets?
Poker is expected value under uncertainty.
Trader interviews test mental arithmetic, probability, expected value and games: what she enjoys.

feedback.correct: Trader. You name your own track in homework 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match what she enjoys to what each role's interviews test.

explain.text: Fast mental games and poker are arithmetic and expected value under time pressure. That is what trader interviews test. You name your own track, for both cycles, in homework 1.

ideas: A trader prices and takes risk; a researcher tests ideas in data; a developer builds the systems.
Interviews test the daily work: trader, arithmetic, probability and games; researcher, statistics, data and coding; developer, coding at speed.
Read a posting's tasks, not its title. Strats at banks mix research and development.

formula.name: Reading a posting
formula.note: The title can mislead. The tasks cannot.

summary.trap: Trading interviews do not test finance knowledge. Firms state none is needed; they test numbers and bets.

quiz.prose: A posting asks the intern to rewrite an order-routing system in C++ and cut its latency.
quiz.question: Which role is this?

options.why: You matched "orders" to trading. Writing the system that sends orders is engineering.
You matched "C++" to quant research. Cutting latency is a developer's job.

feedback.correct: Developer: the system, its code and its speed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the intern will do all day.

explain.text: Rewriting a system in C++ and cutting latency is building software. That is the developer's day, so expect coding rounds.

quiz.question: Which test is a researcher's interview most likely to include?

options.text: An open case: predict a quantity from a dataset and defend the model

options.why: You picked a trader's round. Research interviews are built on data.
You treated research as company analysis. Quant research is statistics on data.
You picked a systems developer's round.

feedback.correct: An open data case is the researcher's signature round.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the test to a day spent in data.

explain.text: Researchers work on open questions in data. Interviews mirror it: statistics, regression, machine learning, coding and an open case.

quiz.prose: A posting is titled "Quantitative Researcher". Its tasks: quote prices to clients through the day and manage the desk's risk.
quiz.question: Which interviews should you prepare for?

options.text: A researcher's: regression and a data case
options.why: You went by the title. The tasks are quoting and risk, which are a trader's.
Nothing in the tasks is building systems.

feedback.correct: The tasks win over the title.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the tasks, not the title.

explain.text: Quoting prices and managing risk are trading tasks. Prepare for a trader's interviews, whatever the title says.

quiz.question: A bank's "strats summer analyst" role is closest to which mix?

options.why: You read "desk" as trading. Strats build the desk's models and code.
Strats are quants, not client sales.

feedback.correct: Models and code: research and development together.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a strat builds.

explain.text: Strats build models and the code that runs them. Reported strats interviews mix probability and maths with coding (l4, October 2026).
